content: 1. The decriminalization of drug use and possession, alongside addressing violence, stigma, and discrimination in healthcare settings, is essential for improving health outcomes. 2. While the primary focus of HIV prevention has been on injecting opioids, there is increasing evidence linking the use of other drugs, such as amphetamine-like stimulants, to heightened sexual risk behaviors and HIV transmission. 3. A specific form of drug use during sexual activity, known as chemsex, significantly increases the risk of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including hepatitis C virus (HCV) transmission. 4. Integrating STI and family planning services within HIV care settings is recommended, though the evidence supporting this is of very low certainty. 5. For men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender individuals, periodic testing for asymptomatic urethral and rectal infections caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis using nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) is suggested over not offering such testing. 6. Periodic testing for asymptomatic syphilis infection in MSM and transgender individuals is strongly recommended over not offering such screening, supported by moderate-certainty evidence. 7. For female sex workers in lowand middle-income countries, periodic screening for asymptomatic STIs is suggested, though the evidence is of low certainty. 8. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis during their first antenatal care visit, regardless of the prevalence of syphilis in the setting. 9. Management of urethral discharge should be based on the results of quality-assured molecular assays. In settings with limited molecular testing capacity, syndromic treatment is recommended to ensure same-day treatment. 10. For vaginal discharge, treatment for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and/or Trichomonas vaginalis should be provided during the same visit. Molecular assay results can guide treatment where feasible. 11. In settings with limited molecular testing, treatment based on rapid point-of-care tests or syndromic management is suggested. 12. Treatment for bacterial vaginosis is recommended if vaginal discharge is present or based on microscopy results, if available. 13. For candidiasis, treatment is suggested based on the type of discharge (e.g., curd-like with vaginal itching) or microscopy results, if available. 14. Sexually active women presenting with lower abdominal pain should be assessed for pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and treated syndromically if clinical features such as cervical motion tenderness or lower abdominal tenderness are present. 15. Testing for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and, if available, Mycoplasma genitalium is recommended to support partner management. 16. For genital ulcers, including anorectal ulcers, treatment should be based on quality-assured molecular assays. In settings with limited testing capacity, syndromic treatment is recommended to ensure same-day care. 17. Anorectal discharge management should also rely on molecular assay results, but syndromic treatment is recommended in resource-limited settings. 18. Good clinical practices for men include taking a detailed medical and sexual history, performing genital and anal examinations, offering HIV and syphilis testing, and ensuring partner notification and treatment history are reviewed for persistent symptoms. 19. For women, good practices include taking a medical and sexual history, performing abdominal and pelvic examinations, assessing for PID, and offering HIV and syphilis testing. Persistent or recurrent vaginal discharge should prompt referral to a center with laboratory capacity for further diagnosis. 20. The syndemics model highlights the interaction of concurrent epidemics, such as HIV and STIs, which amplify each other’s impact, particularly in vulnerable populations. 21. Many STIs are asymptomatic, especially in women, and evidence shows that STIs increase both the transmissibility and acquisition risk of HIV. 22. Infection with N. gonorrhoeae significantly increases HIV-1 shedding in seminal fluid, while genital herpes (HSV-2) nearly triples the risk of acquiring HIV. 23. HIV-seropositive women are at high risk of infection with oncogenic types of human papillomavirus (HPV). 24. Diagnosing and treating STIs is a priority to reduce HIV transmission and optimize sexual and reproductive health. 25. Strengthening STI prevention, screening, diagnosis, and treatment is critical, as syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis remain the most common STIs. 26. High STI prevalence is reported among users of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), particularly MSM, at baseline and during PrEP use. 27. A comprehensive approach to sexual and reproductive health for people living with HIV includes appropriate STI services, screening, and treatment. 28. Syndromic management of symptomatic STIs should be complemented by etiological diagnosis where feasible. 29. Safer sex practices, including condom use, should be promoted to prevent future STIs. 30. STI treatment should include partner management to ensure comprehensive care. 31. For people with urethral discharge, vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain, anorectal discharge, or genital ulcers, management should ideally be based on molecular assay results. In resource-limited settings, syndromic treatment is recommended. 32. Anorectal infections are prevalent among individuals engaging in anal intercourse, with asymptomatic infections being common in high-risk groups such as MSM, sex workers, and transgender individuals. 33. Recommendations for syphilis treatment in pregnant women and congenital syphilis have been updated and reprinted by WHO. 34. Integrating STI services within HIV care settings is a key strategy to increase service coverage for people living with HIV. 35. Addressing stigma and discrimination in healthcare is essential to improve health-seeking behavior and public health efforts to control HIV and STI epidemics. 36. Healthcare providers should offer culturally competent and sensitive STI care to encourage vulnerable populations to seek clinical services. 37. Immunizations are an important component of HIV care, and people living with HIV should be assessed for vaccination eligibility at all stages of care. 38. Vaccines are generally safer and more effective in people living with HIV who are on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and have a CD4 count above 200 cells/mm³. 39. People with severe immunosuppression may face higher risks from live attenuated vaccines, while inactivated vaccines may require supplemental doses or revaccination after immune recovery with ART.
